quote: advocating that the Internet would “wake up” and become an AI when it became “sufficiently complex.”
content: Scaling laws are the opposite of "sufficient complexity does it." They are quantitative relations between compute, data, parameters and loss, found by measurement, for a specific architecture with a specific objective — which is to say someone did the work of saying how, in equations, and the equations make predictions that were used to allocate budgets before the models were trained. The prediction the essay was arguing against was that the Internet would wake up spontaneously once it got complicated enough, and that did not happen and is not what happened. "Train a particular architecture on a particular corpus at a particular scale" is a mechanism; "sufficient complexity" is the absence of one.

quote: How would an AI invent for itself the concept of an “operator,” or “macro,” which is the key to solving the Rubik’s Cube?
content: The solver is a mechanism, and the essay asked for a mechanism. DeepCubeA works by approximate value iteration from the goal state to produce a learned heuristic, then A* search over that heuristic — a specification precise enough to reimplement (Agostinelli et al. 2019), and its learned value function encodes the distance structure that hand-coded macro operators were built to exploit. What the essay was refusing was not the claim that a learning system could do it; it was the answer "complexity" given in place of any account at all. The history supplied a better answer than the essay expected, in the form the essay demanded.

quote: That was when I thought to myself, “Maybe this one is teachable.”
content: What Marcello produced was the application of a distinction to a new case, unprompted, which is the transfer test the sequence endorses everywhere. The password failure mode is producing a term with nothing attached; Marcello caught himself using a word as a placeholder and said so, which requires having the concept rather than the word. The essay is explicit that the moment of interest is his noticing, not his vocabulary. A student who spots his own semantic stopsign has done the thing the previous essays asked for.
